blocks.text: **The problem.** A **peak** is an element strictly greater than its neighbours. Given an array `nums` where no two neighbours are equal, return the index of **any** peak. Treat the positions just outside the array as `-∞`, so the first or last element can be a peak too. Your solution must run in **O(log n)** time.

blocks.alt: A chart of [1, 2, 3, 1]. The value 3 at index 2 is higher than both neighbours, so it is a peak.

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]
Output: 2     nums[2] = 3 is bigger than 2 and 1

Input:  nums = [1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]
Output: 1 or 5     both 2 and 6 are peaks; either index is accepted

blocks.text: Picture the array as a mountain range: each value is a height. A peak is any point higher than the points on both sides. Because the edges count as `-∞`, a peak **always** exists — even a steadily rising array ends in one (its last element).
The problem asks for **any** peak, not the highest one. That freedom is what makes an O(log n) solution possible.
1. Brute force: check every index against its neighbours
Test the definition directly: an index is a peak if it beats its left neighbour **and** its right neighbour, where a missing neighbour (off the edge) counts as `-∞`.
**Time O(n), space O(1).** Correct, but it ignores the problem's demand for **O(log n)**.
2. Optimal: walk until the line goes down

We don't need to check the left neighbour at all. Scan from the left: as long as the values keep rising, we're climbing. The first time `nums[i] > nums[i + 1]`, index `i` is a peak — we got there uphill, and the next step goes down. If that never happens, the array only rises and the last index is the peak.

**Time O(n), space O(1).** Still linear in the worst case, but it uses one comparison per step — and a much more useful idea: **if the line is going up, a peak lies ahead**. The best solution takes that idea and jumps instead of walking.
3. Best solution: binary search on the slope
Stand at the middle index `mid` and look one step right. There are only two possibilities:

blocks.alt: Two charts. Left: at mid the line goes uphill to the right, so a peak must lie to the right. Right: at mid the line goes downhill to the right, so a peak lies at mid or to its left.

elements.text: uphill → a peak is to the right
elements.originalText: uphill → a peak is to the right

elements.text: downhill → peak at mid or left
elements.originalText: downhill → peak at mid or left

items: **Uphill** (`nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`): keep climbing right and you must reach a peak — either the line turns down somewhere, or you reach the last element, which beats the `-∞` beyond it. So a peak exists in the **right half**: `low = mid + 1`.
**Downhill** (`nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1]`): by the same argument walking left, a peak exists at `mid` or to its left: `high = mid`. (`mid` itself stays in range — it might be the peak.)

blocks.text: Each step throws away half of the range, and a peak is always kept inside it. When `low` meets `high`, that index is a peak. This is **binary search** — not on sorted values, but on the direction of the slope.

blocks.caption: The bars show the heights. Watch the range (unfaded bars) halve each step. Try an always-rising array: the search runs straight to the last index.

blocks.text: `mid + 1` is always a valid index here: the loop only runs while `low < high`, so `mid` is at most `high - 1`. In Java and C++, `low + (high - low) / 2` avoids overflow on huge arrays.
**Time O(log n), space O(1).** The range halves every step: for a million elements that's about 20 steps instead of a million.

rows.approach: Brute force: check every index against its neighbours
rows.timeWhy: Each of the **n** indexes is compared with its two neighbours.

rows.approach: Optimal: walk until the line goes down
rows.timeWhy: In the worst case the line rises to the **last** element, so every step is walked.

rows.approach: Best: binary search on the slope
rows.timeWhy: Each comparison **halves** the range, so about **log₂ n** steps.

items: **Strictly increasing** — `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`: the last index is the peak.
**Strictly decreasing** — `[100, 80, 60, 50, 20]`: the first index is the peak.
**Several peaks** — any of them is a correct answer.

blocks.text: Binary search works whenever you can look at the middle and decide which half **must** contain an answer. Searching on a property rather than on sorted values also finds the minimum of a rotated sorted array, and the smallest capacity or speed that "works" in scheduling problems.
